    Cell-Type-Level Test for Heterogeneity in Disease Relevance

    cell_type_heterogeneity.Rd

    Tests whether the cells within a cell type differ from one another in disease relevance, giving one p-value per cell type. Summarising a cell type by its mean score discards this question, which is often the biologically interesting part.

    cell_type_heterogeneity(
  topic_res,
  enrichment,
  Sigma,
  groups,
  min_cells = 20,
  p_adjust_method = "BH"
)

    Arguments

    topic_res

    Topic-model results with Pmat (peaks x topics) and Lmat (cells x topics), as returned by run_fastTopics().

    enrichment

    Length-K vector of topic enrichment estimates.

    Sigma

    K x K covariance of enrichment; the Sigma element of ldsc_jackknife_cov().

    groups

    Character or factor vector of cell-type labels, one per cell, in the row order of topic_res$Lmat. NA labels are dropped.

    min_cells

    Groups smaller than this are skipped. Default 20.

    p_adjust_method

    Passed to stats::p.adjust(). Default "BH".

    Value

    A data frame with one row per cell type: cell_type, n, stat (\(T_g\)), p, fdr, sorted by p-value.

    The statistic

    The cell score is linear in the topic enrichments, \(s_i = w_i' E\) with \(\sum_k w_{ik} = 1\), where the weights depend only on the cell's topic loadings and the topic annotation sizes. For cell type \(g\), with \(S_g\) the covariance of \(w\) across its cells, the within-type variance of the score is a quadratic form, $$T_g = \mathrm{Var}_g(s) = \hat E' S_g \hat E.$$

    The null

    The null of no heterogeneity is that all topics are equally enriched, \(E = c \mathbf{1}\) for some unknown \(c\). This is not the null of no enrichment: if every topic carries the same enrichment, every cell scores \(c\) and the within-type variance is zero whatever the loadings. Because the weights sum to one, \(S_g \mathbf{1} = 0\) exactly, so writing \(\hat E = c\mathbf{1} + \varepsilon\) removes every term in \(c\) and $$T_g = \varepsilon' S_g \varepsilon \sim \sum_j \lambda_j \chi^2_1,$$ with \(\lambda\) the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma^{1/2} S_g \Sigma^{1/2}\). The p-value is exact by Imhof inversion; no permutation is involved. That \(c\) drops out matters in practice, since every topic annotation is open chromatin and therefore genuinely enriched.

    Choice of Sigma

    Use ldsc_jackknife_cov(). The annotation-correlation approximation is not adequate here: the statistic is orthogonal to the constant direction, which is exactly where that approximation errs, and on null simulations it makes the test conservative at every threshold. The test is also sensitive to the level of the off-diagonal correlation, so an exchangeable stand-in is not a substitute for the full matrix.

    Interpretation

    \(T_g\) and its null eigenvalues both scale linearly with \(S_g\), so the p-value is invariant to the overall size of the within-group loading spread. Power depends on whether the direction in which cells vary within a group aligns with the direction in which topic enrichments differ. A cell type's score range therefore does not predict whether it will be called heterogeneous, and a range-based summary will legitimately disagree with these calls.

    Interpret heterogeneity only for cell types that pass the association test: heterogeneity within a cell type carrying no overall signal is heterogeneity in noise. The test also conditions on the topic loadings as fixed, ignoring topic-model uncertainty, as the cell score variance does.

    See also

    ldsc_jackknife_cov(), get_cs()
